FXUS62 KRAH 101757
AFDRAH

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Raleigh NC
157 PM EDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

* No significant changes from previous forecast thinking

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 215 PM Thursday...

1) Hot temperatures to persist through the end of the week, with 
limited cooling this weekend. Warm temperature return next week. 

2) Unsettled weather returns Friday and Saturday with a Marginal 
Risk for excessive rain (flash flooding). 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 157 PM Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... Hot temperatures to persist through the end of the 
week, with limited cooling this weekend. Warm temperature return 
next week. 

Early afternoon water vapor imagery reveals an upper ridge 
positioned off the SC coast, with a similarly strong (594dm) ridge 
over the Southwest US. In between, a weak longwave trough stretched 
from MI to MO which was slowly dragging a surface cold front into 
the Ohio Valley. Ahead of this front across NC, temperatures have 
warmed and dewpoints have risen quite a bit with heat index values 
approaching the triple digits in many locations south and east of 
the Triangle.

The front will be slow to approach the area, keeping NC within the 
pre-frontal warm sector through Friday. As such, increased heat 
index values near or slightly above 100 degrees will be common 
through tomorrow, with the highest values across the Triangle and 
points southeast. Deep BL mixing Friday afternoon will allow 
dewpoints to retreat slightly into the lower 70s which should keep 
obs several degrees below Heat Advisory criteria, although those who 
are sensitive to the heat should take the proper precautions through 
the end of the week.

As the front approaches the area on Saturday, it'll wash out and/or 
retreat back northward early next week. Cloud cover will keep 
temperatures in check with highs Saturday and Sunday in the 
mid/upper 80s. The front will result in slightly lower thicknesses 
and dewpoints across NC next week, but still with highs in the upper 
80s to lower 90s. Dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s should keep heat 
index values in the low to mid 90s. 


KEY MESSAGE 2... Unsettled weather returns Friday and Saturday with 
a Marginal Risk for excessive rain (flash flooding). 

As mentioned above, a slow moving cold front will approach from the 
west on Friday before stalling out, then washing out, Saturday into 
Sunday. Pre-frontal moisture advection will promote dewpoints in the 
low to mid 70s Friday and Saturday and there should be enough 
instability to support scattered shower and thunderstorm 
development. The best jet dynamics will be displaced well to our 
north and with the decaying nature of the surface boundary, 
organized severe convection looks to be limited in nature. The 
increase in moisture and relatively slow moving nature of any storms 
that develop will support an isolated risk of flash flooding, and 
nearly all of central NC remains within a WPC Marginal Risk of 
excessive rainfall. A few HREF LPMM bullseyes of more than 2" are 
present across the Coastal Plain Friday afternoon, although I would 
anticipate more areal coverage and localized heavy precip potential 
on Saturday given the nearby proximity of the decaying surface 
boundary. By Sunday the front should be non-existent with convection 
becoming more isolated and less organized.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z THURSDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/... 
As of 157 PM Thursday...

Most of central NC should generally remain VFR through the 24 hour 
TAF period. Over the next few hours this afternoon, a few 
southwesterly gusts will remain in the north. Gusts look like they 
should only reach up to 20 kts. Tonight, there could be a brief 
period of restrictions as it looks like an area of low stratus/fog 
could develop in the southern Coastal Plain and Sandhills. 
Confidence is low in this happening, but models seem to be trending 
towards a greater probability, so added a TEMPO at FAY, with 
restrictions being possible at RWI as well. Friday afternoon, there 
could be isolated to scattered showers/thunderstorms across the 
region, however the best chance of this looks to be after 18Z. 

Outlook: Shower and thunderstorm chances are possible each 
afternoon/evening through the weekend, with the best chance for 
widespread rain Saturday. Additionally, low stratus and/or fog may 
develop and cause sub-VFR restrictions the next several mornings.

&&

.RAH WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...Leins
AVIATION...Helock

FXUS62 KILM 101837
AFDILM

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Wilmington NC
237 PM EDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
No significant changes have been made to the forecast over the
weekend into early next week.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Shower and thunderstorm chances will increase this weekend.

2) Heat and humidity will build and heat indices should exceed 
100 degrees through Monday.

3) Grand Strand minor coastal flooding is possible during 
multiple high tides over the coming days.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Shower and thunderstorm chances will increase 
this weekend.

Models look broadly similar to yesterday showing the persistent
mid and upper level ridge across the Southeast U.S. breaking
down this weekend as a shortwave digs into the mid-Mississippi
Valley region. This will remove the subsidence inversion that's
been capping us for days, and establish a deeper flow of Gulf
moisture that should bring precipitable water value up toward
2.2 inches by Saturday.

Today's isolated showers are being vertically inhibited by warm,
dry conditions aloft within the upper ridge. Once that factor 
is removed this weekend, forecast rain chances blossom: 20-40 
percent Friday, 60-80 percent on Saturday, and 50-60 percent on 
Sunday. 

None of these days appear to be washouts and model storm-total 
QPF through Sunday appears to have decreased in spots from 
yesterday. A few lucky locations should still pick up 2-3 inch 
totals over the coming days, with half inch totals likely more 
common. Storm mode should remain single-cell with 0-6 km bulk 
shear 10 knots or less. Loose storm organization along outflow 
boundaries and the seabreeze front should occur.

Storm coverage should begin to decline Monday as the 700-500 mb
ridge redevelops just to our west, intercepting the flow of Gulf
moisture. The subsidence inversion reappears in forecast
soundings by Tuesday which should lead to much drier conditions
Tuesday and Wednesday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Heat and humidity will build and heat indices should 
exceed 100 degrees through Monday.

Light south to southwest low level winds should advect plenty 
of Atlantic and Gulf moisture across the Carolinas through the 
weekend. Dewpoints remaining in the 70s coupled with well-above 
normal high temperatures in the lower to middle 90s should equal
heat indices rising above 100 degrees each day through Monday. 

Tomorrow (Friday) appears to be the hottest day of the period. 
Forecast 850 mb temps near +19C are 4C above normal and 1.5C 
above the 90th climatological percentile at the KMHX upper air 
site. Our current forecast high for Friday is still 4-5 degrees
F below daily records.

This unseasonably hot airmass should remain across the area
through Monday, but will be tempered by additional clouds and 
precipitation. By Tuesday, Canadian high pressure moving across 
New England should introduce a northeasterly low level flow 
which should bring a slightly cooler marine airmass onshore with
forecast highs generally in the 85-90 degree range Tuesday and 
Wednesday.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Minor Grand Strand coastal flooding is possible 
during multiple high tides over the coming days.

September's New Moon occurs today which is leading to a period
of larger astronomical tides. Tidal anomalies along the Grand
Strand beaches as measured at Myrtle Beach's Springmaid Pier
should average around +1.0 feet today through the weekend. Half
to two-thirds of this anomaly is likely due to sea level rise 
leaving onshore winds responsible for the remainder. 

Forecast water levels should exceed flood stage at Springmaid
Pier by about 0.3 feet this evening, and may reach or slightly
exceed flood stage during high tides Friday morning through 
Sunday morning. See the recently-issued Coastal Flood Advisory 
for details.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z THURSDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
An area of showers offshore is spreading broken low
stratocumulus back toward the Grand Strand coastline. There is 
a low probability of ceiling impacts at KMYR and KCRE between 
18-20z before the offshore showers weaken or dissipate. New 
convective showers are developing inland along and west of the 
South Carolina seabreeze front this afternoon, but the 
probability of impacts on airports is too low for mention in the
TAFs at this time.

Isolated showers should dissipate this evening and VFR
conditions are expected overnight. New convective showers may 
begin to develop again Friday along the seabreeze front prior 
to 18z.

Extended Outlook... Although VFR conditions will prevail, there
is increasing potential for pop-up showers and thunderstorms
bringing brief MVFR/IFR conditions, especially Saturday and
Sunday. There is also a low potential for late night/early
morning stratus or ground fog, particularly affecting KLBT and
KFLO Saturday and Sunday.

&&

.MARINE...
Tonight through Tuesday...High pressure off the Southeast coast
is weakening as a cold front moves southward. This front is
still expected to stall across interior North Carolina Friday
night before lifting back to the north Saturday. South to
southwesterly winds should continue with speeds less than 15
knots. 

Increasing coverage of showers and thunderstorms is expected
beginning late Friday night as Gulf moisture increases across 
the area, and as high pressure aloft dissipates and is replaced 
by cyclonic flow ahead of an upper level trough to our west.
Rather high chances for showers and storms should continue until
Monday when high pressure should begin to redevelop aloft.

&&

.ILM WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
NC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 9 PM this evening to midnight EDT 
     tonight for NCZ107.
SC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 7 PM to 10 PM EDT this evening for 
     SCZ054-056.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Jacksonville FL
241 PM EDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

For the latest NE FL and SE GA Daily Key Messages please visit:
https:/www.weather.gov/media/jax/briefings/nws-jax-briefing.pdf

- Strong Storms and Localized Flooding Possible through Early
  this Evening, Mainly at Inland Locations.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk at All Area Beaches.

- Heat Index Values Peak in the 103-108 Degree Range Each
  Afternoon through Monday

- Scattered to Numerous Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms from
  Friday through Tuesday.

&&

.NEAR TERM /THROUGH TONIGHT/...

Main Highlights through Tonight:

- Strong Storms and Localized Flooding Possible through Early
  this Evening, Mainly at Inland Locations.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk at All Area Beaches.

Afternoon surface analysis depicts Atlantic high pressure (1022 
millibars) centered near Bermuda and extending its axis 
southwestward across our area. Meanwhile, a cold front extends 
from New England through the Ohio Valley and the Mid-Mississippi
Valley. Aloft...deep-layered ridging was positioned along the 
southeastern seaboard, with troughing progressing eastward 
across the Great Lakes and Mid-Mississippi Valleys. Otherwise, 
troughing was developing over central and western portions of 
the Gulf, or along the western periphery of the Atlantic ridge 
axis. Latest GOES-East derived Total Precipitable Water imagery 
indicates that deep tropical moisture remains in place for 
locations along and south of I-10, where PWATs were in the 2.1 -
2.4 inch range, while values north of I-10 were generally in 
the 1.9 - 2.1 inch range. High moisture levels and low level 
flow veering to a more south or south-southwesterly direction 
since yesterday have fostered scattered to numerous showers and 
a few embedded thunderstorms along the I-95 corridor early this 
afternoon, with activity mostly isolated thus far over the 
Suwannee Valley and the I-10 corridor, as well as along the U.S.
Highway 301 corridor in southeast GA. Temperatures at 19Z have 
climbed to the upper 80s and lower 90s outside of areas impacted
by convection, with dewpoints in the 70s at inland locations 
and closer to 80 at coastal locations.

Gradually cooling temperatures aloft and the presence of deep  
tropical moisture should allow for convection to increase in 
coverage and intensity as the afternoon progresses. Convective 
outflows should merge at inland locations during the mid to late 
afternoon hours, especially for locations between the I-75 and
I-95 corridors in northeast and north central FL, with 
outflows then progressing northward and increasing thunderstorm 
coverage and intensity over the Okefenokee Swamp in interior 
southeast GA late this afternoon through the evening hours. 
Mesoscale boundary collisions should allow for convection to 
"pulse" and become briefly strong at inland locations, with 
stronger storms capable of producing downburst winds of 40-55 
mph, along with frequent lightning strikes and torrential 
downpours, with localized flooding possible due to relatively 
slow storm motion. Low level flow veering to southwesterly this 
evening could bring at least scattered convection back towards 
the I-95 corridor this evening, with activity weakening by the 
mid-evening hours tonight. 

Debris cloud cover will tend to thin out after midnight, with 
southwesterly flow potentially developing some predawn convection 
along the FL Big Bend and Nature Coasts, but activity is not 
expected to cross the Suwannee River before sunrise. Fog and low 
stratus ceilings could develop over portions of interior southeast 
GA. Low level southwesterly flow will keep lows in the 70s area-
wide.

&&

.SHORT TERM /FRIDAY THROUGH SATURDAY NIGHT/...

Main Highlights This Period:

- Daily potential for isolated strong thunderstorms and
  localized flooding.

The local area remains located on the western periphery of
surface high pressure over the Atlantic with weak high 
pressure aloft through the weekend. Southwesterly to southerly 
low level winds will remain in place, and will continue to pump 
deep moisture (PWATs 2- 2.3") into the area. With ample moisture
in place, the weak subsidence associated with the mid/upper 
ridging will not be strong enough to suppress convection. Expect
scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms to develop each
day, mainly during the afternoon and evening hours. The 
steering flow will allow for the Gulf breeze to move well inland
each afternoon, with mergers with the Atlantic sea breeze 
occurring between the US-301 corridor towards the I-95 corridor.
With the elevated moisture aloft, showers and storms that do 
develop could bring periods of heavy rainfall and localized 
flooding. Isolated strong storms, maybe a few severe storms, 
could bring gusty winds in the 30 to 50 mph range along boundary
mergers. 

Daytime highs will be in the low-mid 90s along inland locations
on Friday and Saturday with highs in the upper 80s to around 
90 along the coast. Overnight Lows will be in the lower to mid 
70s. Heat index values will hover just under Heat Advisory 
criteria, with values in the upper 90s to around 107F.

&&

.LONG TERM /SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...

Main Highlights This Period Saturday through Wednesday: 

- Daily Thunderstorms Potential Each Day Next Week.

- Elevated Rip Current Risk Next Week. 

By Monday, the high pressure axis will shift north resulting in
a return to an onshore flow regime which will persist through 
the work week. Deep moisture remain in place with PWAT values 
above 2 inches persisting through at least Tuesday. This will 
continue to result in scattered to numerous showers and storms 
each day with localized flooding concerns and some potential for
strong thunderstorms along boundary collisions. As we move into
the middle to latter part of the work week, PWAT values will 
fall to seasonable around 1.75 inches. In response, expect rain 
chances to fall slightly with coverage becoming more scattered 
Wednesday and Thursday. 

The onshore flow will also cause afternoon temperatures to cool 
slightly, generally topping out in the 85-90 degree range most 
places by Tuesday and Wednesday. Lows in the 70s will persist.

Rip current risk will also become elevated rather than moderate
as a result of the pattern shift.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z THURSDAY THROUGH 18Z FRIDAY/...

Showers and thunderstorms will continue to impact the Duval
County terminals and SSI through around 22Z. Periods of IFR to
LIFR visibilities will be possible during heavier downpours, 
with brief surface wind gusts of 25-30 knots possible, 
especially with stronger storms near VQQ after 19Z. TEMPO groups
were used at these terminals, as a couple of rounds of 
convection will be possible this afternoon. Activity will then 
spread to the GNV terminal after 20Z, where a TEMPO group for 
brief surface wind gusts up to 30 knots and IFR conditions 
during heavier downpours will be possible through around 00Z. 
Convection should stay west of the SGJ terminal through around 
23Z, but a round of early evening convection will be possible. 
Confidence was only high enough for a PROB30 group at this time,
with brief surface wind gusts up to 25 knots and MVFR 
conditions possible during heavier downpours through around 03Z 
Friday. VFR conditions should then prevail at the regional 
terminals by 04Z. Periods of IFR to LIFR conditions are then 
expected to develop at VQQ after 06Z. VFR conditions are then 
forecast at the regional terminals after 12Z Friday, with brief 
periods of MVFR ceilings possible after 15Z.

&&

.MARINE...

Showers and thunderstorms will continue to impact mainly the
near shore coastal waters through the early evening hours 
tonight. Otherwise, Atlantic high pressure centered near Bermuda
this afternoon will shift southward while gradually weakening 
on Friday as a frontal boundary shifts towards the southeastern 
states. This front will stall and weaken well to the north of 
our local waters this weekend. Prevailing winds will become 
southwesterly from Friday through the upcoming weekend, with the
afternoon sea breeze shifting winds to southeasterly each 
afternoon across the near shore waters. Showers and 
thunderstorms developing over coastal locations during the 
afternoon hours will shift eastward across our local waters 
during the late afternoon and evening hours from Friday through 
the upcoming weekend. High pressure will then build down the 
southeastern seaboard early next week, with onshore winds 
forecast to develop by Monday afternoon, with breezy conditions 
and building seas forecast towards Tuesday and Wednesday of next
week.

Rip Currents: Diminished winds and dropping surf will tend to
lower the rip current risk toward the moderate range today. 
Prevailing winds will become south-southwesterly by Friday, with
a lingering easterly ocean swell and onshore winds developing 
during the afternoon hours behind the inland moving sea breeze 
keeping a lower- end moderate risk at area beaches.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...

Winds will steadily veer to become southerly to southwesterly
this afternoon. This will allow for the Gulf Coast and Atlantic
Coast sea breezes to push inland by the afternoon hours, with 
showers and storms developing and increasing in coverage near 
Highway 301. As weaker transport winds develop, dispersions will
be Fair over the next few days. Otherwise, RH values will sit 
at Good levels through the weekend as moisture moves in from the
Gulf and towards southeast Georgia and northeast Florida. 

Fog Potential: Gusty and erratic wind shifts will occur from  
thunderstorm activity. Patchy fog is expected across inland areas 
the next couple of mornings, with widespread dense fog unlikely. 

&&

.HYDROLOGY...

As far as coastal water levels, we expect tidal water levels to
peak to near the Action stage through Friday due to the recent
onshore flow but mainly due to the new moon phase which is 
Friday, Sept 11th. Mostly nuisance type flooding is expected for
a brief time into the weekend, including in the St Johns River 
Basin.

As far as rainfall today, isolated pockets of about 4 inches are 
possible mainly across an area from eastern Marion county 
northward to around Baker county. These storms may cause 
temporary flooding, especially in any poor drainage or urbanized
areas.

&&

.PRELIMINARY POINT TEMPS/POPS...
AMG  73  92  73  92 /  50  40  20  50 
SSI  77  90  77  90 /  40  50  20  50 
JAX  75  92  74  92 /  60  60  20  70 
SGJ  76  90  75  90 /  50  50  20  70 
GNV  74  91  73  91 /  50  60  20  70 
OCF  74  92  74  92 /  50  60  20  70 

&&

.JAX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
FL...None.
GA...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

FXUS65 KBOU 101740
AFDBOU

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
1140 AM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Mainly dry through Friday with warmer temperatures.

- Return to more unsettled pattern this weekend with a chance of
  thunderstorms especially on Sunday. Cooler Saturday, then warmer
  on Sunday.

- Another cold front moves into the area next Monday or Tuesday
  with a chance of showers and thunderstorms.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Wednesday/...
Issued at 240 AM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026

The flow aloft will remain WNW today as southerly level flow is 
across the plains.  MLCAPE will rise up to 1000 j/kg over portions 
of the far ern plains by aftn.  Chances for tstms still look on the 
low side as I can't find a focus for activity.  However, can't rule 
out an isold storm or two mainly across Lincoln county where a weak 
convergence zone will exist this aftn.  Meanwhile, temps will begin 
to warm as readings reach the upper 80's to lower 90's over nern CO.

On Fri, zonal flow aloft will be over the area as a sfc lee trough 
develops over the plains.  This will lead to another warm day as 
highs rise into the upper 80's to mid 90's over the plains. 
Meanwhile, models have some mid level moisture embedded in the flow, 
which may lead to isold high based showers/tstms over the higher 
terrain in the aftn.  Across the plains, MLCAPE is under 500 j/kg so 
any threat of showers/tstms will be on the low side.

For Fri night into Sat, zonal flow aloft will continue.  Meanwhile, 
a cold front will move across Fri night into Sat morning.  This 
front will drop temps back to more seasonal levels across nern CO. 
MLCAPE is fcst to be in the 500-800 j/kg across the plains with 
lower values across the higher terrain.  For now, have kept in a 
slight chc for showers/tstms across the higher terrain and along the 
I-25 Corridor for the aftn/evening hours.  Highs over nern CO will 
be in the upper 70's to mid 80's.

By Sun, an upper level trough will move into the nrn Rockies with 
increasing WSW flow aloft across the area.  At the sfc, a lee trough 
will intensify east of the mtns with SSE low level flow across the 
plains.  MLCAPE is fcst to increase to 1000-1500 j/kg over portions 
of the plains east of a pseudo dryline. Thus may see a few 
strong/svr storms by late aftn thru the evening hours. Highs on 
Sun, will likely rise back to above normal levels.

Looking ahead to Mon, WSW flow aloft will remain over the area. 
Models have backed off on the timing of another cold front moving 
across as they now show it moving in Mon night into Tue morning.  If 
this front does hold off until Mon night, then another day of above 
normal temps would occur over the plains.  Meanwhile, may have a 
better chc of showers/tstms across the plains Mon night into Tue 
morning as position of upper level jet combines with upslope flow 
behind the front.  

For Tue, differences exist between the ECMWF and GFS with respect to 
timing of additional precip and temps.  The ECMWF has a cool and 
stable airmass, over the plains, with highs only in the mid 60's to 
lower 70s.  Meanwhile, the GFS isn't as cool and has far more 
precip.   

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Friday/...
Issued at 1129 AM MDT Thu Sep 10 2026

VFR conditions will prevail for all terminals through the TAF
period. This afternoon, expect moderate ESE/SE winds to prevail
across the Denver metro. Winds will rotate clockwise towards
drainage flow beginning near 03Z (+/1 hr), with S wind speeds
increasing for KDEN and KAPA to 12-16 kts. Expect KBJC to
transition to lighter westerly flow. Tomorrow, light and variable
winds < 10 kts in the morning, particularly after 15-16Z. There
will be some mid-level moisture in place Friday afternoon, with a
very slight chance (~15%) of an isolated high-based shower and
gusty outflow after 22-23Z. With almost no instability to work 
with, confidence in such activity is low and thus not included in 
the KDEN TAF.

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...RPK
AVIATION...BRQ
